key_claim: The Sahara swings between wet grassland and dry desert, and each swing pushes plants and animals around and may split species apart.

slides.body: In long wet periods, the Sahara and Arabia turn into savanna grassland. Lakes grow, more rivers flow, and African plants and animals become common there.

slides.headline: Then it dries, and life moves out
slides.body: Rivers shrink to dry wadis. Plants and animals retreat north, south or east, some along the Nile Valley, then on toward Asia.

slides.headline: Splitting groups may make new species
slides.body: Moving apart can separate some species into different climates. They must adapt, which may possibly lead to new species over time.

slides.headline: The Sahara works like a pump.
slides.body: Wet and dry swings push life around, and may split species apart.

caption:
The Sahara keeps flipping between green and desert.

In long wet periods, the Sahara and Arabia become savanna grassland, with larger lakes and more rivers. African plants and animals become common there.

The catch? The rains retreat. Lakes fall, rivers become dry wadis, and plants and animals move north, south or east, some along the Nile Valley toward Asia.

The payoff? That can split some species into different climates, forcing them to adapt. It may even give rise to new species. It's called the Sahara pump theory.

Source: Wikipedia — Sahara pump theory
